- $X(n):$ $n$ is less than $10$

- $Y(n):$ $n$ is less than $13$

- $Z(n):$ $n$ is an integer" :question/worked-solution "The word "and" is represented by the symbol "$∧,$" while the word "or" is represented by the symbol "$∨.$"

Note that this sentence consists of two parts:  

- **Part 1:** $n$ is less than $10$ or $13.$ This corresponds to

$$
{{n\text{ is less than }10}_{⏟}}_{X}\,{{\text{or}}_{⏟}}_{∨}\,{{n\text{ is less than }13}_{⏟}}_{Y},
$$

that is, $X∨Y.$

- **Part 2:** $n$ is an integer. This corresponds to $Z.$

$$
{{n\text{ is less than }10\text{ or }13}_{⏟}}_{X∨Y}\,{{\text{and}}_{⏟}}_{∧}\,{{n\text{ is an integer}}_{⏟}}_{Z},
$$

- The **conjunction** of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$ is a new predicate which we denote as follows: 

$$
P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \land Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)
$$

This conjunction is true whenever $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is true *and* $Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$ is true for a specific set of respective variable assignments. The conjunction is false if either $P$ or $Q$ is false.

- The **disjunction** of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$ is written as follows:

$$
P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \lor Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)
$$

This disjunction is true whenever $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is true, $Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$ is true, or both are true, for a specific set of variable assignments. The disjunction is false if $P$ *and* $Q$ are false.

For example, consider the following predicates:

- $P(n):$ $n$ is even

- $Q(n):$ $n$ is positive

Then, $P(n) \land Q(n)$ is a new predicate that reads "$n$ is even *and* $n$ is positive," which can be simplified to "$n$ is even and positive."

On the other hand, $P(n) \lor Q(n)$ is a new predicate that reads "$n$ is even *or* $n$ is positive," which can be simplified to "$n$ is even or positive."

When it's clear that $P(n)$ is a predicate in the variable $n,$ we sometimes omit the variables when writing them. So, $P(n) \land Q(n)$ and $P(n) \lor Q(n)$ can be written as $P \land Q$ and $P \lor Q,$ respectively." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199521 :tutorial/content "Let $T_P$ and $T_Q$ be the truth sets of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),$ respectively. Note that we're assuming our predicates have the same universal set.

From the definition of the conjunction of predicates, we have that $P \land Q$ is true if both $P$ and $Q$ are true. Therefore, the truth set of $P \land Q$ is the *intersection* of the truth sets of $P$ and $Q{:}$

$$
T_{P \land Q} = T_P \cap T_Q
$$

For example, consider the following predicates defined over the set of positive integers:

- $P(x):$ $x$ is divisible by $3$

- $Q(x):$ $24$ is divisible by $x$

We start by finding the truth sets of $P(x)$ and $Q(x){:}$

- The truth set of $P(x)$ is 

$$
T_P = \big\{ 3,6,9,12,15,18,21,24,27 \ldots \big\}.
$$

- The truth set of $Q(x)$ is 

$$
T_Q = \big\{ 1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24 \big\}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{P∧Q} & ={T}_{P}\cap {T}_{Q} \\  & =\{3,6,9,12,15,18,21,24,27…\}\cap \{1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24\} \\  & =\{3,6,12,24\}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199542 :tutorial/content "Once again, let $T_P$ and $T_Q$ be the truth sets of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),$ respectively. 

From the definition of the disjunction of predicates, we have that $P \lor Q$ is true if $P$ is true, or $Q$ is true, or both are true. Therefore, the truth set of $P \lor Q$ must be the *union* of the truth sets of $P$ and $Q{:}$

$$
T_{P \lor Q} = T_P \cup T_Q
$$

For example, suppose we are given the following shaded regions that represent the truth sets of the predicates $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y),$ defined over the universal set $\mathbb{R}^2.$ 

![](images/ce/ce71e62503acd1c82f6bba7e1d9c83c40f0a98f04c689c3ccd58e7a99a814856.png)

To get the truth set of $P(x,y) \lor Q(x,y),$ we take all the points that belong to $T_P$ or $T_Q,$ as shown below.

![](images/9c/9c528c5fe390bd1f22cb473c01b768e83f5b3a35d97eb7e670c6734b8cb2c2f8.png)

**Note:** The points where the *dashed* line meets the *solid* curve belong to $T_P \cup T_Q$ since these points lie in $T_P.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199523 :tutorial/content "Conjunction and disjunction of predicates are generalizations of logical operations on statements. Moreover, the properties of these operations on statements can be translated to corresponding operations on predicates. 

In particular, the idempotent, absorption, associative, and commutative laws also apply to conjunction and disjunction of predicates. 

So, for predicates $P(x_1,x_2\ldots,x_n),$ $Q(y_1,y_2\ldots,y_m),$ and $R(z_1,z_2\ldots,z_p),$ we have the following:

- *The Idempotent Laws*: 

$$
\begin{aligned}P∧P≡P∨P≡P\end{aligned}
$$

- *The Associative Laws*:

$$
\begin{aligned}P∧(Q∧R) & ≡(P∧Q)∧R \\ P∨(Q∨R) & ≡(P∨Q)∨R\end{aligned}
$$

- *The Commutative Laws*:

$$
\begin{aligned}P∧Q & ≡Q∧P \\ P∨Q & ≡Q∨P\end{aligned}
$$

- *The Distributive Laws*:

$$
\begin{aligned}P∧(Q∨R) & ≡(P∧Q)∨(P∧R) \\ P∨(Q∧R) & ≡(P∨Q)∧(P∨R)\end{aligned}
$$

- *The Absorption Laws*:

$$
\begin{aligned}P∧(P∨Q) & ≡P \\ P∨(P∧Q) & ≡P\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198514 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

- The **conjunction** of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$ is a new predicate which we denote as follows: 

$$
P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \land Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)
$$

This conjunction is true whenever $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is true *and* $Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$ is true for a specific set of respective variable assignments. The conjunction is false if either $P$ or $Q$ is false.

- The **disjunction** of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$ is written as follows:

$$
P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \lor Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)
$$

This disjunction is true whenever $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is true, $Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$ is true, or both are true, for a specific set of variable assignments. The disjunction is false if $P$ *and* $Q$ are false.

For example, consider the following predicates:

- $P(n):$ $n$ is even

- $Q(n):$ $n$ is positive

Then, $P(n) \land Q(n)$ is a new predicate that reads "$n$ is even *and* $n$ is positive," which can be simplified to "$n$ is even and positive."

On the other hand, $P(n) \lor Q(n)$ is a new predicate that reads "$n$ is even *or* $n$ is positive," which can be simplified to "$n$ is even or positive."

When it's clear that $P(n)$ is a predicate in the variable $n,$ we sometimes omit the variables when writing them. So, $P(n) \land Q(n)$ and $P(n) \lor Q(n)$ can be written as $P \land Q$ and $P \lor Q,$ respectively." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199521 :tutorial/content "Let $T_P$ and $T_Q$ be the truth sets of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),$ respectively. Note that we're assuming our predicates have the same universal set.

From the definition of the conjunction of predicates, we have that $P \land Q$ is true if both $P$ and $Q$ are true. Therefore, the truth set of $P \land Q$ is the *intersection* of the truth sets of $P$ and $Q{:}$

$$
T_{P \land Q} = T_P \cap T_Q
$$

For example, consider the following predicates defined over the set of positive integers:

- $P(x):$ $x$ is divisible by $3$

- $Q(x):$ $24$ is divisible by $x$

We start by finding the truth sets of $P(x)$ and $Q(x){:}$

- The truth set of $P(x)$ is 

$$
T_P = \big\{ 3,6,9,12,15,18,21,24,27 \ldots \big\}.
$$

- The truth set of $Q(x)$ is 

$$
T_Q = \big\{ 1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24 \big\}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{P∧Q} & ={T}_{P}\cap {T}_{Q} \\  & =\{3,6,9,12,15,18,21,24,27…\}\cap \{1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24\} \\  & =\{3,6,12,24\}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199542 :tutorial/content "Once again, let $T_P$ and $T_Q$ be the truth sets of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),$ respectively. 

From the definition of the disjunction of predicates, we have that $P \lor Q$ is true if $P$ is true, or $Q$ is true, or both are true. Therefore, the truth set of $P \lor Q$ must be the *union* of the truth sets of $P$ and $Q{:}$

$$
T_{P \lor Q} = T_P \cup T_Q
$$

For example, suppose we are given the following shaded regions that represent the truth sets of the predicates $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y),$ defined over the universal set $\mathbb{R}^2.$ 

![](images/ce/ce71e62503acd1c82f6bba7e1d9c83c40f0a98f04c689c3ccd58e7a99a814856.png)

To get the truth set of $P(x,y) \lor Q(x,y),$ we take all the points that belong to $T_P$ or $T_Q,$ as shown below.

![](images/9c/9c528c5fe390bd1f22cb473c01b768e83f5b3a35d97eb7e670c6734b8cb2c2f8.png)

**Note:** The points where the *dashed* line meets the *solid* curve belong to $T_P \cup T_Q$ since these points lie in $T_P.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199523 :tutorial/content "Conjunction and disjunction of predicates are generalizations of logical operations on statements. Moreover, the properties of these operations on statements can be translated to corresponding operations on predicates. 

In particular, the idempotent, absorption, associative, and commutative laws also apply to conjunction and disjunction of predicates. 

So, for predicates $P(x_1,x_2\ldots,x_n),$ $Q(y_1,y_2\ldots,y_m),$ and $R(z_1,z_2\ldots,z_p),$ we have the following:

- *The Idempotent Laws*: 

$$
\begin{aligned}P∧P≡P∨P≡P\end{aligned}
$$

- *The Associative Laws*:

$$
\begin{aligned}P∧(Q∧R) & ≡(P∧Q)∧R \\ P∨(Q∨R) & ≡(P∨Q)∨R\end{aligned}
$$

- *The Commutative Laws*:

$$
\begin{aligned}P∧Q & ≡Q∧P \\ P∨Q & ≡Q∨P\end{aligned}
$$

- *The Distributive Laws*:

$$
\begin{aligned}P∧(Q∨R) & ≡(P∧Q)∨(P∧R) \\ P∨(Q∧R) & ≡(P∨Q)∧(P∨R)\end{aligned}
$$

- *The Absorption Laws*:

$$
\begin{aligned}P∧(P∨Q) & ≡P \\ P∨(P∧Q) & ≡P\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198514 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [[17592186198099 :question/worked-solution "The word "and" is represented by the symbol "$\land.$"

"question-0d9b6544-a3d6-5482-a66b-0b543948f593"] [17592186199520 :tutorial/content "We can apply the logical operations of conjunction and disjunction to predicates.

- The **conjunction** of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$ is a new predicate which we denote as follows: 

$$
P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \land Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)
$$

This conjunction is true whenever $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is true *and* $Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$ is true for a specific set of respective variable assignments. The conjunction is false if either $P$ or $Q$ is false.

- The **disjunction** of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$ is written as follows:

$$
P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \lor Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)
$$

This disjunction is true whenever $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is true, $Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$ is true, or both are true, for a specific set of variable assignments. The disjunction is false if $P$ *and* $Q$ are false.

For example, consider the following predicates:

- $P(n):$ $n$ is even

- $Q(n):$ $n$ is positive

Then, $P(n) \land Q(n)$ is a new predicate that reads "$n$ is even *and* $n$ is positive," which can be simplified to "$n$ is even and positive."

On the other hand, $P(n) \lor Q(n)$ is a new predicate that reads "$n$ is even *or* $n$ is positive," which can be simplified to "$n$ is even or positive."

When it's clear that $P(n)$ is a predicate in the variable $n,$ we sometimes omit the variables when writing them. So, $P(n) \land Q(n)$ and $P(n) \lor Q(n)$ can be written as $P \land Q$ and $P \lor Q,$ respectively."] [17592186199521 :tutorial/content "Let $T_P$ and $T_Q$ be the truth sets of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),$ respectively. Note that we're assuming our predicates have the same universal set.

From the definition of the conjunction of predicates, we have that $P \land Q$ is true if both $P$ and $Q$ are true. Therefore, the truth set of $P \land Q$ is the *intersection* of the truth sets of $P$ and $Q{:}$

$$
T_{P \land Q} = T_P \cap T_Q
$$

For example, consider the following predicates defined over the set of positive integers:

- $P(x):$ $x$ is divisible by $3$

- $Q(x):$ $24$ is divisible by $x$

We start by finding the truth sets of $P(x)$ and $Q(x){:}$

- The truth set of $P(x)$ is 

$$
T_P = \big\{ 3,6,9,12,15,18,21,24,27 \ldots \big\}.
$$

- The truth set of $Q(x)$ is 

$$
T_Q = \big\{ 1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24 \big\}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{P∧Q} & ={T}_{P}\cap {T}_{Q} \\  & =\{3,6,9,12,15,18,21,24,27…\}\cap \{1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24\} \\  & =\{3,6,12,24\}.\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186199542 :tutorial/content "Once again, let $T_P$ and $T_Q$ be the truth sets of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),$ respectively. 

From the definition of the disjunction of predicates, we have that $P \lor Q$ is true if $P$ is true, or $Q$ is true, or both are true. Therefore, the truth set of $P \lor Q$ must be the *union* of the truth sets of $P$ and $Q{:}$

$$
T_{P \lor Q} = T_P \cup T_Q
$$

For example, suppose we are given the following shaded regions that represent the truth sets of the predicates $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y),$ defined over the universal set $\mathbb{R}^2.$ 

![](images/ce/ce71e62503acd1c82f6bba7e1d9c83c40f0a98f04c689c3ccd58e7a99a814856.png)

To get the truth set of $P(x,y) \lor Q(x,y),$ we take all the points that belong to $T_P$ or $T_Q,$ as shown below.

![](images/9c/9c528c5fe390bd1f22cb473c01b768e83f5b3a35d97eb7e670c6734b8cb2c2f8.png)

**Note:** The points where the *dashed* line meets the *solid* curve belong to $T_P \cup T_Q$ since these points lie in $T_P.$"] [17592186199523 :tutorial/content "Conjunction and disjunction of predicates are generalizations of logical operations on statements. Moreover, the properties of these operations on statements can be translated to corresponding operations on predicates. 

In particular, the idempotent, absorption, associative, and commutative laws also apply to conjunction and disjunction of predicates. 

So, for predicates $P(x_1,x_2\ldots,x_n),$ $Q(y_1,y_2\ldots,y_m),$ and $R(z_1,z_2\ldots,z_p),$ we have the following:

- *The Idempotent Laws*: 

$$
\begin{aligned}P∧P≡P∨P≡P\end{aligned}
$$

- *The Associative Laws*:

$$
\begin{aligned}P∧(Q∧R) & ≡(P∧Q)∧R \\ P∨(Q∨R) & ≡(P∨Q)∨R\end{aligned}
$$

- *The Commutative Laws*:

$$
\begin{aligned}P∧Q & ≡Q∧P \\ P∨Q & ≡Q∨P\end{aligned}
$$

- *The Distributive Laws*:

$$
\begin{aligned}P∧(Q∨R) & ≡(P∧Q)∨(P∧R) \\ P∨(Q∧R) & ≡(P∨Q)∧(P∨R)\end{aligned}
$$

- *The Absorption Laws*:

$$

- To find the the truth set of $P(x),$ we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-1 & <5 \\ 3x & <6 \\ x & <2\end{aligned}
$$

 
So, the truth set of $P(x)$ is
$T_P = (-\infty,2).$

- The truth set of $Q(x)$ is 
$T_Q = [3,\infty).$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{P∨Q} & ={T}_{P}\cup {T}_{Q} \\  & =(-\infty ,2)\cup [3,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048592} {:db/id 17592186198704 :question/id #uuid "67540ebf-2612-5ae3-8a6d-03d5320b1acb" :question/math-academy-id "q-171558"} {:db/id 17592186198705 :question/id #uuid :tutorial/content "We can apply the logical operations of conjunction and disjunction to predicates.

- The **conjunction** of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$ is a new predicate which we denote as follows: $$P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \land Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$$ This conjunction is true whenever $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is true *and* $Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$ is true for a specific set of respective variable assignments. The conjunction is false if either $P$ or $Q$ is false.
- The **disjunction** of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$ is written as follows: $$P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \lor Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$$ This disjunction is true whenever $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is true, $Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$ is true, or both are true, for a specific set of variable assignments. The disjunction is false if $P$ *and* $Q$ are false.

For example, consider the following predicates:

- $P(n):$ $n$ is even
- $Q(n):$ $n$ is positive

Then, $P(n) \land Q(n)$ is a new predicate that reads "$n$ is even *and* $n$ is positive," which can be simplified to "$n$ is even and positive."

On the other hand, $P(n) \lor Q(n)$ is a new predicate that reads "$n$ is even *or* $n$ is positive," which can be simplified to "$n$ is even or positive."

When it's clear that $P(n)$ is a predicate in the variable $n,$ we sometimes omit the variables when writing them. So, $P(n) \land Q(n)$ and $P(n) \lor Q(n)$ can be written as $P \land Q$ and $P \lor Q,$ respectively." :tutorial/id #uuid "c05b0e9a-b514-5c42-9d07-7ec2466b30be" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7984 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b041ca76-9538-556f-ba42-756566d8edf6" :step/math-academy-id 120115 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199040}} {:db/id 17592186199040 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198252 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198099 :question/id #uuid "d40cb0df-fce7-5236-b0ef-62f5a343b3a3" :question/math-academy-id "e-12724"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2993b4ab-e45b-579a-8a11-b5e9ee107d5b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048778}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198689} {:db/id 17592186198690} {:db/id 17592186381368} {:db/id 17592186381495} {:db/id 17592186389656}] :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Compound Predicate in Symbolic Form"} :step/id #uuid "8701928d-1944-5363-b962-b4891f892daa" :step/math-academy-id 120116 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199041}} {:db/id 17592186199041 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198253 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198100 :question/id #uuid "3e2319b4-ab10-50ef-845b-9586c9761227" :question/math-academy-id "e-12725"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ce659c55-ca26-52c6-b15e-ec317013d856" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198691} {:db/id 17592186198692} {:db/id 17592186381375} {:db/id 17592186381382} {:db/id 17592186381502} {:db/id 17592186389670} {:db/id 17592186389710}] :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Nested Compound Predicate in Symbolic Form"} :step/id #uuid "77ba67c1-cc43-57be-ac98-62a769bb7e42" :step/math-academy-id 120119 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199042}} {:db/id 17592186199042 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199521 :tutorial/content "Let $T_P$ and $T_Q$ be the truth sets of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),$ respectively. Note that we're assuming our predicates have the same universal set.

From the definition of the conjunction of predicates, we have that $P \land Q$ is true if both $P$ and $Q$ are true. Therefore, the truth set of $P \land Q$ is the *intersection* of the truth sets of $P$ and $Q{:}$

$$T_{P \land Q} = T_P \cap T_Q$$

For example, consider the following predicates defined over the set of positive integers:

- $P(x):$ $x$ is divisible by $3$
- $Q(x):$ $24$ is divisible by $x$

We start by finding the truth sets of $P(x)$ and $Q(x){:}$

- The truth set of $P(x)$ is $$T_P = \big\{ 3,6,9,12,15,18,21,24,27 \ldots \big\}.$$
- The truth set of $Q(x)$ is $$T_Q = \big\{ 1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24 \big\}.$$

Therefore, we have

$$\begin{aligned}{T}_{P∧Q} & ={T}_{P}\cap {T}_{Q} \\ & ={3,6,9,12,15,18,21,24,27…}\cap {1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24} \\ & ={3,6,12,24}.\end{aligned}$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "74eb89b1-6654-56b5-9fef-718a3acfcb2f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7985 :tutorial/title "The Truth Set of a Conjunction"} :step/id #uuid "ea6a5438-89a7-508e-92fb-e311fd2c5c48" :step/math-academy-id 120122 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199043}} {:db/id 17592186199043 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199542 :tutorial/content "Once again, let $T_P$ and $T_Q$ be the truth sets of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),$ respectively.

From the definition of the disjunction of predicates, we have that $P \lor Q$ is true if $P$ is true, or $Q$ is true, or both are true. Therefore, the truth set of $P \lor Q$ must be the *union* of the truth sets of $P$ and $Q{:}$

$$T_{P \lor Q} = T_P \cup T_Q$$

For example, suppose we are given the following shaded regions that represent the truth sets of the predicates $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y),$ defined over the universal set $\mathbb{R}^2.$

![](images/ce/ce71e62503acd1c82f6bba7e1d9c83c40f0a98f04c689c3ccd58e7a99a814856.png)

To get the truth set of $P(x,y) \lor Q(x,y),$ we take all the points that belong to $T_P$ or $T_Q,$ as shown below.

![](images/9c/9c528c5fe390bd1f22cb473c01b768e83f5b3a35d97eb7e670c6734b8cb2c2f8.png)

**Note:** The points where the *dashed* line meets the *solid* curve belong to $T_P \cup T_Q$ since these points lie in $T_P.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4d1b797a-ff89-514d-a0df-87d6858b45e3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8140 :tutorial/title "The Truth Set of a Disjunction"} :step/id #uuid "9905e635-bc99-5ab6-8557-95a009250e4e" :step/math-academy-id 120123 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199044}} {:db/id 17592186199044 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198254 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198101 :question/id #uuid "3a115dd5-3241-5627-bb40-121b75eeb7ae" :question/math-academy-id "e-12726"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e6bc626a-9517-584c-bf55-8653227f830e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048592}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198704} {:db/id 17592186198705} {:db/id 17592186381410} {:db/id 17592186381551} {:db/id 17592186381579} {:db/id 17592186389783} {:db/id 17592186389790}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Truth Sets of Conjunctions and Disjunctions"} :step/id #uuid "69f763bb-fe3d-5367-b28c-7de5d1163729" :step/math-academy-id 120124 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199045}} {:db/id 17592186199045 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199523 :tutorial/content "Conjunction and disjunction of predicates are generalizations of logical operations on statements. Moreover, the properties of these operations on statements can be translated to corresponding operations on predicates.

In particular, the idempotent, absorption, associative, and commutative laws also apply to conjunction and disjunction of predicates.

So, for predicates $P(x_1,x_2\ldots,x_n),$ $Q(y_1,y_2\ldots,y_m),$ and $R(z_1,z_2\ldots,z_p),$ we have the following:

- *The Idempotent Laws*: $$\begin{aligned}P∧P≡P∨P≡P\end{aligned}$$
- *The Associative Laws*: $$\begin{aligned}P∧(Q∧R) & ≡(P∧Q)∧R \\ P∨(Q∨R) & ≡(P∨Q)∨R\end{aligned}$$
- *The Commutative Laws*: $$\begin{aligned}P∧Q & ≡Q∧P \\ P∨Q & ≡Q∨P\end{aligned}$$
- *The Distributive Laws*: $$\begin{aligned}P∧(Q∨R) & ≡(P∧Q)∨(P∧R) \\ P∨(Q∧R) & ≡(P∨Q)∧(P∨R)\end{aligned}$$

- The **conjunction** of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$ is a new predicate which we denote as follows: $$P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \land Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$$ This conjunction is true whenever $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is true *and* $Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$ is true for a specific set of respective variable assignments. The conjunction is false if either $P$ or $Q$ is false.

- $P(n):$ $n$ is even
- $Q(n):$ $n$ is positive

Then, $P(n) \land Q(n)$ is a new predicate that reads "$n$ is even *and* $n$ is positive," which can be simplified to "$n$ is even and positive."

On the other hand, $P(n) \lor Q(n)$ is a new predicate that reads "$n$ is even *or* $n$ is positive," which can be simplified to "$n$ is even or positive."

When it's clear that $P(n)$ is a predicate in the variable $n,$ we sometimes omit the variables when writing them. Note that we're assuming our predicates have the same universal set.

From the definition of the conjunction of predicates, we have that $P \land Q$ is true if both $P$ and $Q$ are true. Therefore, the truth set of $P \land Q$ is the *intersection* of the truth sets of $P$ and $Q{:}$

$$T_{P \land Q} = T_P \cap T_Q$$

For example, consider the following predicates defined over the set of positive integers:

- $P(x):$ $x$ is divisible by $3$
- $Q(x):$ $24$ is divisible by $x$

- The truth set of $Q(x)$ is $$T_Q = \big\{ 1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24 \big\}.$$

- *The Absorption Laws*: $$\begin{aligned}P∧(P∨Q) & ≡P \\ P∨(P∧Q) & ≡P\end{aligned}$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6ad96982-4e36-52f9-816a-db64ba277433" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7989 :tutorial/title "Laws Involving Conjunction and Disjunction of Predicates"} :step/id #uuid "71a8a715-2397-5052-a148-b7cc79853a2b" :step/math-academy-id 120128 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199046}} {:db/id 17592186199523 :tutorial/content "Conjunction and disjunction of predicates are generalizations of logical operations on statements. mathematical tools required to study modern machine learning.
This course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics.
